questions.question: Distinguish between standard of living and quality of life, and list four indicators used to measure the standard of living.
questions.expected_answer: Standard of living is the level of material well-being, measured by the quantity and quality of goods and services a person or household can obtain; it depends mainly on income and access to services. Quality of life is broader and includes non-material factors such as health, safety, freedom, clean environment, leisure and community relationships. Indicators: income per person (GDP per capita); access to piped water, electricity and sanitation; type of dwelling; school enrolment and literacy; life expectancy and infant mortality; share of income spent on food; the Human Development Index.

questions.question: Compare modern urban and rural lifestyles in South Africa under the headings: income and employment, access to services, cost of living, and community.
questions.expected_answer: Income and employment: urban — more varied and better-paid wage jobs; rural — subsistence and small-scale farming, farm work, grants and remittances, fewer jobs. Access to services: urban — better access to piped water, electricity, sanitation, clinics, schools, banks, internet; rural — longer distances, communal taps, gravel roads, weaker connectivity. Cost of living: urban — higher rent, transport and food costs, everything bought; rural — often own home and land, grow some food, lower costs. Community: urban — weaker extended family networks, more crime and pollution but more diversity; rural — strong family and community networks, cleaner environment.

questions.question: Define urbanisation, give two push and two pull factors, and explain one positive and one negative effect on cities and on rural areas.
questions.expected_answer: Urbanisation is the movement of people from rural to urban areas, increasing the share of the population living in towns and cities. Push: lack of jobs, poor services, drought, land shortages. Pull: job opportunities, better schools and health care, modern amenities. Cities: positive — more workers and consumers, higher productivity; negative — informal settlements, overloaded services, urban unemployment. Rural areas: positive — remittances sent home; negative — loss of young working-age adults and skills, fields left unplanted.
